proposed_edits.old_text: As agents are expected to solve broader and more complex tasks, they rely on external knowledge saved as skills to handle tasks beyond the LLM’s parametric capabilities. As the skill corpora grows into hundreds or thousands of skills, skill routing becomes a bottleneck, where the agent must efficiently retrieve and select the appropriate skills to complete a task. Recent skill routing approaches leverage task feedback to improve skill routing performance online. However, feedback-driven updates to routing criteria can regress performance, and accumulating task feedback at scale requires efficient experience management. We introduce a recursive self-improving algorithm for skill routing in a black-box setting called RouterBSI. It refines task applicability predicates using Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) with bounded replay to minimize errors on seen tasks and a held-out validation gate to reduce regressions on unseen tasks. The router evaluates predicates for top-k retrieved skills then selects skills if the task satisfies their respective predicate. RouterBSI improves its cold-start top-5 recall of required skills by 24.9% across different retrievers on tasks from TheoremQA, LogicBench, ToolQA, MedCalc-Bench, CHAMP, and BigCodeBench sharing a 26k skill corpus. On average, it retains 90.5% of the required skills in top 5 from the top 50 skills retrieved.
proposed_edits.new_text: Skill routing must distinguish a reusable skill’s applicability from its topical similarity to a task. RouterBSI refines one natural-language applicability predicate per skill without updating language-model weights. It selects revisions by empirical Boolean loss on bounded, current-inclusive replay and applies an iteration-end validation gate against cold-start predicates. These checks do not guarantee monotonic improvement over previously accepted predicates or future tasks. We study six SRA-Bench collections using 748 held-out tasks involving skills represented in training, within a 26,262-skill retrieval corpus. In the current exploratory comparison, RouterBSI has the highest observed aggregate nDCG@1 and nDCG@10 among the reported router rows. Retention is normalized to each method’s own retrieval coverage, and improved routing does not establish uniform downstream gains. The paper-facing manifests mark load-bearing results nonreportable, so these observations require provenance resolution before they can support confirmatory claims.

proposed_edits.old_text: We presented RouterBSI, a non-parametric framework that refines explicit skill applicability predicates from routing failures without updating model weights. It combines minimum Bayes risk selection over bounded replay with held-out validation. Experiments on six SRA-Bench datasets show that RouterBSI achieves the strongest average routing performance among evaluated methods and preserves more required skills as the selection budget decreases. Ablations support the complementary contributions of replay and validation and show improvements across model backbones. These findings demonstrate the value of editable predicates for feedback-driven skill routing, although stronger routing does not consistently yield the best downstream performance. Future work can incorporate skill dependencies to better connect skill selection with downstream task requirements.
proposed_edits.new_text: RouterBSI refines explicit skill-applicability predicates from labeled routing failures without updating model weights. The current six-benchmark results provide exploratory observations of routing gains; their nonreportable source status prevents confirmatory conclusions until execution and protocol bindings are resolved. Unpaired initialization limits component attribution, and routing gains do not consistently produce the best downstream success.
